research_question: Explain historical causes of irregular English spelling, including sound change, borrowing, scribal conventions, printing, and standardization.

sources.title: Notes on the History of English Spelling
sources.reliability: Peer-reviewed scholarly journal article by Richard L. Venezky
notes: English spelling reflects multiple historical influences rather than one consistent reform.
Spelling conventions were shaped by scribal practices and contact with Old French and Latin.
The history of letter use and sound change helps explain apparent irregularities.

sources.title: Blame the Printing Press
sources.reliability: Academic book chapter from Oxford University Press
notes: Printing in England expanded while spoken English vowels were undergoing major changes.
Printing helped stabilize some spellings even as pronunciation continued to evolve.
Earlier written standards and printers' choices contributed to modern conventions.

sources.title: Johnson's dictionary (1755)
sources.publisher: Examining the OED, University of Oxford
notes: Samuel Johnson's 1755 dictionary became highly influential in English lexicography.
The dictionary used quotations to document and illustrate meanings and word history.
Dictionaries helped codify usage, but they did not erase the historical diversity of spelling.

sources.title: History of English
notes: The Great Vowel Shift reorganized long vowels in English during the late Middle and early Modern English periods.
Sound change created mismatches between established spellings and later pronunciations.
The vowel shift involved several linked changes rather than a single uniform event.

sources.title: The Making of the Oxford English Dictionary
sources.reliability: Academic historical study by an Oxford English Dictionary associate editor
notes: The OED developed from nineteenth-century efforts to collect historical evidence for English words.
Its first printed fascicle appeared in 1884 and the first edition was completed in 1928.
Historical dictionaries record variation and development rather than imposing a fully phonetic spelling system.
